claims.text: Equiatomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC alloy.
Adding no more than 5 at.% V to NbMoTaW will improve its room-temperature ductility.
Adding no more than 5 at.% V will not significantly compromise the alloy's high-temperature mechanical strength.
Adding no more than 5 at.% V will not significantly compromise the alloy's irradiation resistance.
V atoms will randomly substitute into the NbMoTaW BCC lattice.
The V-modified alloy will remain a single-phase BCC solid solution.
V substitution will reduce lattice friction stress in NbMoTaW.
V substitution will reduce the Peierls barrier in NbMoTaW.
Reduced lattice friction and Peierls barrier will facilitate room-temperature dislocation motion.
Facilitated dislocation motion will increase room-temperature elongation to failure or otherwise reduce brittleness.
High configurational entropy and similar atomic radii will preserve BCC phase stability after V addition.
Preservation of the BCC phase will maintain high-temperature strength.
V has irradiation tolerance comparable to the other refractory elements in NbMoTaW.
The V-modified alloy will retain yield strength and creep resistance similar to untreated NbMoTaW at 1600 °C.
The V-modified alloy will exhibit defect accumulation and swelling rates comparable to untreated NbMoTaW after irradiation.
V content must remain at or below 5 at.% to avoid phase separation or excessive lattice distortion.
Single-phase BCC retention after alloying is a boundary condition for the hypothesis.
Failure to improve room-temperature ductility, or significant degradation of high-temperature strength or irradiation resistance, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Calling the product 'near-equiatomic NbMoTaWV' is compositionally ambiguous: a five-element near-equiatomic alloy would contain about 20 at.% V, whereas the intervention and boundary restrict V to no more than 5 at.%. The wording is consistent only if 'near-equiatomic' refers to the four parent elements rather than all five.
